title: Aditir devāḥ: the Earth, mother of all beings
theme: A litany of the Earth as Aditi, mother of gods, men, ancestors and demons alike, ending with the words of the seer Vasiṣṭha: she is true, she is immortal.

words.context: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa: «अदितिशब्दोऽखण्डितेति व्युत्पत्त्या भूमिमाचष्टे» — Aditi, ‘the unbroken’, names the earth

words.role: first of the five kinds of beings named
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «देवादयः पञ्च जातिविशेषा अदितिरूपाः» — gods and the rest, five kinds of being, are forms of Aditi
The anonymous commentator: «देहोपादानत्वादियमदितिर्माता जननी» — mother, because she is the material of their bodies
The anonymous commentator: «मेदिनी मधुकैटभमेदसा जाता» — born of the marrow of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, «अथवा मेदस्विनी कठिनेत्यर्थः» — or simply firm; Bhāskara: «मेदिनी स्नेहवती» — rich, unctuous

words.gram: as printed (instr. sg. in form); read by all the commentators as f. nom. sg. mahatī
words.context: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa: «महती गुणाधिका» — great in qualities; Bhāskara: «महती महापरिमाणा» — great in extent
Sāyaṇa: «सावित्री सवितुः प्रेरकस्यान्तर्यामिणः संबन्धिनी» — belonging to Savitṛ, the inner ruler who impels

words.meaning: Gāyatrī — the protector of those who sing
words.context: Sāyaṇa: «गायत्री गायकान्स्वोपासकांस्त्रायते रक्षतीत्यर्थः» — she protects those who sing her praise
Sāyaṇa: «जगती जगदाश्रयभूता» — the support of the world
Sāyaṇa: «पृथ्व्यनेकविस्तारवती» — spread out in many ways
Sāyaṇa: «बहुला निबिडावयवा» — of dense parts; Bhāskara: «बहुला बहूनामर्थानां लात्री» — the giver of many things
Sāyaṇa: «विश्वा सर्वात्मिका» — the self of all
Sāyaṇa: «भूता प्राणिदेहोत्पत्तेः पूर्वमेव विद्यमाना» — existing before the bodies of living beings arose; Bhāskara: «भूता महाभूतात्मिका» — of the nature of the great element

words.meaning: which? — the one hard to name
words.context: Sāyaṇa: «कतमाऽतिशयेन सुखरूपा» — supremely pleasant; Bhāskara: «कतमा अशक्यनिर्धारणा» — impossible to pin down

words.base: काया (for the commentators; Bhāskara reads का या)
words.meaning: embodied — she who becomes all bodies
words.context: Sāyaṇa: «काया सर्वप्राणिदेहरूपेण परिणता» — transformed into the bodies of all beings
Sāyaṇa: «सत्या व्यवहारदशायां बाधरहिता» — not contradicted in the world of experience
Sāyaṇa: «तथैवामृता मरणरहिता» — and likewise free from death
The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa: «इत्येवं वसिष्ठो महामुनिराह» — so says the great sage Vasiṣṭha

sandhi.type: visarga after i; -āḥ before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: aditiḥ + devāḥ → aditir devāḥ (the visarga after i becomes r before a voiced sound); -āḥ loses its visarga before a voiced consonant (P. 8.3.22 (हलि सर्वेषाम्)): devā gandharvā manuṣyāḥ.
pitaraḥ + asurāḥ → pitaro ’surāḥ (P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति)); the visarga becomes s before t (P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः)): asurās teṣām.
satyā + iti → satyeti and amṛtā + iti → amṛteti (a/ā + i gives e, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः)); iti + amṛtā → ity amṛtā (P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि)).

morphology.note: The base and the Ānandāśrama text print mahatā, in form an instrumental; the Tirupati e-text has mahatī, and all three commentators gloss mahatī (‘great’), the nominative that the list of epithets requires. The collation classes the Tirupati reading as a witness error because the other two agree; it may rather preserve the sense the commentators read.

The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa take kāyā as one word, ‘she who becomes all bodies’. Bhāskara divides it, kā yā: ‘who [she is], unmanifest; whatever she is, so she is, true’ («का अव्यक्तरूपा या यादृशी भवति सा तादृशी सती सत्या»).

For the anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa the sage Vasiṣṭha, the seer of the mantra: «अतोऽस्य मन्त्रस्य वसिष्ठ ऋषिरित्यर्थः». Bhāskara takes it also as the superlative ‘most excellent’: the knower of Brahman is the truly excellent one, «ब्रह्मज्ञो जनो वसिष्ठ एव भवति».

translation.literal: Aditi — the gods, gandharvas, humans, ancestors and asuras: of them, of all beings, [she is] the mother; the earth, great, the great one, Sāvitrī, Gāyatrī, Jagatī, the wide, the broad, the abundant, the universal, what has come to be, the one hard to name, the embodied — she [is] ‘true’, thus, ‘immortal’, thus [says] Vasiṣṭha.
translation.readable: Aditi, the Earth, is mother of gods, gandharvas, humans, ancestors and asuras — of every being. She is the firm earth, great and worthy of honour; she belongs to Savitṛ, she is Gāyatrī and Jagatī; wide, broad, abundant, all-containing; she was there before all bodies, she cannot be pinned down, and she becomes every body. ‘She is true,’ says Vasiṣṭha, ‘she is immortal.’

syntax: A list of nominatives without a finite verb. Aditi is set at the head, then the five kinds of being whose mother she is (resumed by teṣāṃ sarvabhūtānām), then a long string of feminine epithets. The closing words sā satyā iti amṛtā iti vasiṣṭhaḥ report, with iti, what Vasiṣṭha says of her.

ambiguities.note: Printed as an instrumental, read by every commentator as the nominative mahatī. See the morphology note.
One word (‘embodied’) or two, kā yā (‘who … whatever’): see the morphology note.
The seer’s name, or the superlative ‘most excellent’; Bhāskara reads both.

metre.name: prose
metre.note: A prose litany of 67 syllables in one line.

beginner: This passage praises the Earth under the name Aditi, ‘the unbounded’. It begins by listing the kinds of beings that live on her: gods, celestial musicians, humans, ancestors and the asuras, the gods’ rivals. She is mother of all of them, because every body is made from her. Then comes a long chain of names: the firm one, the great one, the wide, the broad, the abundant, the one that was here before any body was born, the one that becomes all bodies. Some names are those of Vedic metres, Gāyatrī and Jagatī. The passage ends by quoting the sage Vasiṣṭha: she is true, she is immortal. The commentators explain why it stands here: the earth gives food and fields, and so the means to live. It praises; it promises nothing.
analogy: Like the ground under a crowded market: everyone there stands on it, whatever they have come to buy or sell.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It names Aditi as mother of gods, gandharvas, humans, ancestors and asuras — of all beings — gives her many epithets, and reports that Vasiṣṭha calls her true and immortal.

commentary.q: Why a mantra to the Earth here?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa: it is a mantra to the Earth that serves release by way of livelihood, the fields that sustain life: «जीवनहेतुक्षेत्रलाभद्वारा मुक्तिहेतुं पृथिवीदेवताकं मन्त्रमाह» (Sāyaṇa). Bhāskara: it is praise of Brahman in the form of the Earth, «पृथ्वीरूपेण ब्रह्मणस्स्तुतिः», and its last words mean ‘therefore this is the form of Brahman to be worshipped’, «तस्मादिदमेव ब्रह्मणो रूपम् उपास्यमिति वसिष्ठः प्रशस्त आह».

commentary.q: Mother of gods and asuras alike
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The commentators explain that the five kinds named stand for every living body, of which the Earth is the material: «एते च सर्वप्राणिदेहानामुपलक्षकाः» (Sāyaṇa). Bhāskara adds that the five are named for their importance and that birds, snakes and the rest are included: «तेषामन्येषामपि सर्वभूतानां विहगोरगादीनां माता».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Sāyaṇa qualifies: true in the state of worldly dealing, «सत्या व्यवहारदशायां बाधरहिता», and immortal because she endures through the cycle of the four ages: «चतुर्युगपर्यावर्तनेऽप्यवस्थितेत्येतमप्यर्थं वसिष्ठ एवाऽऽह».

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not available here). The anonymous commentator and Sāyaṇa read a mantra to the Earth that supports life and so release; Bhāskara reads praise of Brahman in the Earth’s form.

parallels.note: The Kaṭha also names Aditi, ‘made of all the gods’, born together with the beings — though there the commentators take her differently.

contemporary.text: The passage lists gods, humans and their rivals side by side as children of one Earth, and calls her true and undying. Read today, its plainest lesson is dependence: every kind of being stands on the same ground and is made of it. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: The Earth is called mother of gods and of their rivals alike. What does it mean to have the same mother as one’s opponents?
reflect.deeper: Sāyaṇa says the Earth is ‘true’ in the world of experience. What is gained, and what lost, by qualifying ‘true’ in that way?
reflect.practice: Before a meal, name three things the food passed through on its way to you from the ground.

references.text: Sāyaṇa comments on this mantra as his anuvāka 21 (the concordance maps it correctly), and the anonymous commentator repeats him nearly word for word. Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara’s comment is his anuvāka 21; the edition’s concordance gives no Bhāskara anuvāka for 10.28, so it is cited here by his own number.

flags.note: mahatā (base, Ānandāśrama) against mahatī (Tirupati, and the reading glossed by all three commentators). The collation classes the Tirupati reading as a witness error; it deserves a check against printed editions.
Concordance: Bhāskara’s anuvāka 21 comments on this anuvāka, but the edition’s map lists nothing for 10.28.
The meaning of kāyā (one word or two) and of vasiṣṭhaḥ (name or superlative) differs between the commentators.
